subject: Impute missing covariates in dynocc model (my first NIMBLE)

messages.author: 3205880b9759c04c
messages.subject: Impute missing covariates in dynocc model (my first NIMBLE)
parts:
Dear all,

After last year's AHM course, I have been practicing my modeling skills and reading more about these topics, but want to receive some potential clarifications and recommendations from experts here. 

I am implementing a dynamic occupancy model (dynocc) in NIMBLE (yay!), following the great resource provided by Ken during the course and Mark & Andy influential Ecology paper (2007). With the crossbill dataset example, when the model included covariates, we experienced some problems due to missing values in the covariate "DATE" (specifically in the detection submodel: logit(p[m,j,t] <- rho_0 + rho_date*date[m,j,t], note that I use m as index for site instead of i). Ken implemented a clever solution of imputing missing values as:

# Impute missing dates 
    # (most comments here are OAC trying to learn & understand)
for (m in 1:M){ # loop for each site (m)
    for (t in 1:T){ # loop for each periods (t)
        for (j in 1:J){ # loop for each occasion (j)
            date[m,j,t] ~ dnorm(mu_date, tau_date)
        } # close j
    }  # close t
} # close m

# Priors for imputed parameters
mu_date ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
sigma_date ~ dunif(0, 10)
tau_date <- pow(sigma_date, -2)

Although at that moment it makes a lot of sense to me, I just want to  clarify my interpretation of this, given that it is my first time conducting a Bayesian implementation model. How does the triple "for loop" identify the missing values in date? Should we include a "is.na()" statement somewhere? Could there be a risk of replacing all the original data with this approach? Also, does anyone here know a publication where this imputation procedure is applied to read and cite accordingly? Or any other literature that touches on imputation of missing data?

Thanks!
Orlando

PD. I couldn't find the AHM google group to ask directly there, thanks to the unmarked community for their patience!

Orlando Acevedo-Charry MSc
PhD Candidate - Interdisciplinary Ecology
School of Natural Resource and Environment & 
Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
QuantitativeEcologyLab - Ordway Lab of Ecosystem Conservation
University of Florida

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Impute missing covariates in dynocc model (my first NIMBLE)
parts:
Hi Orlando,

nimble and JAGS handle the missing values automatically. The way I like to think about this is in terms of the direction the information is flowing. If date[m,j,t] is missing, then a sample from the distribution is used to impute it

date[m,j,t] <--- dnorm(mu_date, tau_date)

if date[m,j,t] is not missing, then it is used to help estimate the distribution parameters

date[m,j,t] ---> dnorm(mu_date, tau_date)

I don't know of any specific citations for this, it was a bit of an ad-hoc solution and as such might not be optimal, particularly if the covariate is not actually normally distributed (I don't know if I checked this in the example).

The AHM group is here: https://groups.google.com/g/hmecology

Ken

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Impute missing covariates in dynocc model (my first NIMBLE)
parts:
to add to what Ken says here, this solution that Ken proposed is a standard Bayesian solution (i.e., put a prior on the missing values).  I can't think of a citation off the top of my head but you can look in the standard text books for "missing values" or something and probably find one.
This solution is better than imputing with the mean value of the covariate because it allows for the uncertainty in the missing value and also the structure of the observation model might inform the value of the missing covariate in some models (I'm not sure of this one but, in general, the data could inform you about missing x's).
regards
andy

On Wed, Apr 30, 2025 at 9:32 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
to add to what Ken says here, this solution that Ken proposed is a standard Bayesian solution (i.e., put a prior on the missing values).  I can't think of a citation off the top of my head but you can look in the standard text books for "missing values" or something and probably find one.
This solution is better than imputing with the mean value of the covariate because it allows for the uncertainty in the missing value and also the structure of the observation model might inform the value of the missing covariate in some models (I'm not sure of this one but, in general, the data could inform you about missing x's).

On Wed, Apr 30, 2025 at 9:29 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:
Hi Orlando,

nimble and JAGS handle the missing values automatically. The way I like to think about this is in terms of the direction the information is flowing. If date[m,j,t] is missing, then a sample from the distribution is used to impute it

date[m,j,t] <--- dnorm(mu_date, tau_date)

if date[m,j,t] is not missing, then it is used to help estimate the distribution parameters

date[m,j,t] ---> dnorm(mu_date, tau_date)

I don't know of any specific citations for this, it was a bit of an ad-hoc solution and as such might not be optimal, particularly if the covariate is not actually normally distributed (I don't know if I checked this in the example).

The AHM group is here: https://groups.google.com/g/hmecology

Ken
